t: Sequentially Ordinal Rank Tracker — Pop the Best, Repeatedly
o: **Understanding the problem.** We maintain a growing set of locations ranked by score descending, ties broken by lexicographically smaller name; each `get()` returns the q-th best location where q increments on every call. In the worked example, after adding branford(3) and bradford(2) the first get returns branford; once alps(2) arrives it outranks bradford on the name tie-break, so gets two and three return alps then bradford. Two guarantees shape the design: queries never exceed adds, and each get consumes exactly the next rank. So instead of indexing into a sorted structure we can simply extract the current best element once per `get` — successive extractions are precisely ranks 1, 2, 3, .... With at most $4 \times 10^4$ total calls, both an O(n)-insert sorted array and an O(log n) heap fit easily.
k: Ranking key: higher score first, then smaller name — unique names make it a total order.
get ranks advance one at a time, so popping the current best repeatedly answers every query without index arithmetic.
A heap or balanced BST gives O(log n) per operation; a binary-search-inserted array costs O(n) per add but is simpler.

a.n: Approach 1: Sorted Array With a Query Counter
a.i: Keep one array sorted best-to-worst plus a counter q of gets so far. Each add binary-searches its position under the key (-score, name) and inserts there (O(n) shifting, but cache-friendly). get reads entry q and increments it.
s: Store keys (-score, name) so ascending order equals ranking order.
add(name, score): binary-search the insertion point and insert there.
get(): return data[q].name, then increment q.
a.t: O(n) per add (binary search O(log n) + O(n) shifting), O(1) per get.

a.n: Approach 2: Two Heaps Around the Query Pointer (Optimal)
a.i: Gets consume successive ranks, but a late arrival can deserve a rank that was already handed out (a score-3 location showing up after the 1st best was read). Split locations around the query pointer: reported holds ranks 1..q with its WORST member exposed; pending holds the remainder with its BEST exposed. An arrival better than the worst reported swaps into reported, demoting that worst to pending; anything else lands in pending. Every get promotes pending's best into reported.
s: pending: min-heap keyed (-score, name); reported: min-heap whose root is the WORST already-returned location.
add(name, score): if the newcomer beats reported's worst root, demote that root to pending and insert the newcomer into reported; otherwise push it to pending.
get(): promote pending's best into reported and return its name.
a.t: O(log n) per operation — each add/get touches a constant number of heap (or multiset) nodes; every element crosses the pointer at most once.
a.sp: O(n) — the two structures hold every added location.

w: Say "each get takes the next-best item" early — it collapses this Hard problem into a heap exercise; lead with Approach 2 in an interview and mention Approach 1 as the low-tech fallback. Pitfalls: flipping the name tie-break (smaller name wins even though scores sort descending); re-sorting the whole list on every query; in Java/C++ make sure the comparator orders scores descending. Classic follow-up: support arbitrary rank queries get(i) — switch to an order-statistics tree or SortedList, still O(log n).
